scope_note: Every turn-taking, voice-activity-detection, and endpointing system that decides when a speaker has finished — frame-level VAD models, semantic turn-detection models, the orchestrators that bundle one, and commercial APIs offering endpointing as a feature — on the axes that actually decide whether a voice product feels conversational.
method_note: Nothing here is benchmarked by OpenGauntlet. Figures come from primary sources — vendor docs, model cards, repositories, and papers. 32 of these 35 rows were added through a research-then-adversarial-audit pass instructed to refute rather than confirm before publication, the same discipline applied to the Voices and Listening sections; the remaining 3 (the original seed rows) predate that pass and have not yet been re-audited to the same standard. Latency is this domain's headline number and is quoted here with its source, and with the hardware or frame size where the source states them.

systems.name: NVIDIA Riva (EndpointingConfig / VAD-Based Endpointing)
systems.licence: NVIDIA proprietary (NGC / NVIDIA AI Enterprise licensing terms)
systems.price_note: Riva is primarily consumed as a self-hosted NIM microservice (built and deployed via riva-build/riva-deploy onto your own GPU), not a metered per-minute cloud API in the docs reviewed — so there is no per-minute endpointing charge to report; cost is whatever your NVIDIA AI Enterprise/NGC licensing and GPU hosting already costs.
systems.latency_note: Not published as a fixed latency number; behavior is governed by frame-count windows — start_history (default 300ms window, speech-start flagged at 20% non-blank frames) and stop_history (default 800ms window, speech-end flagged at 98% blank frames), or an alternate neural VAD (Silero: onset 0.85 / offset 0.3 default thresholds).
systems.accuracy_note: Not applicable — this is an endpointing/VAD feature, not a transcription accuracy metric.
systems.languages_note: Not specified for endpointing specifically; Riva's ASR language coverage is documented separately per model and was not independently re-verified here.
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted (NIM container on your own GPU via riva-build/riva-deploy) — not a hosted cloud API in the strict sense, but included here because NVIDIA documents it as a commercial platform feature.
systems.best_for: Organizations that need endpointing logic running entirely on their own infrastructure (data-residency or air-gapped requirements) and are willing to manage GPU-specific model builds.
systems.watch: Riva's own docs warn that deployed model repositories are GPU-architecture-specific — 'always run riva-deploy on the target machine' — a model built and optimized for one GPU generation (e.g. A100) is not guaranteed to work on another (e.g. V100) without rebuilding.
systems.standout: Exposes two entirely different endpointing mechanisms side by side — a classic frame-history threshold algorithm (start_history/stop_history) and a swappable neural VAD (Silero or MarbleNet) — selectable per deployment, including the option to disable endpointing entirely (endpointing_type=none).
systems.billing_unit: Not a metered per-minute API in the docs reviewed — licensed as part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise / NGC self-hosted deployment.
systems.self_host: Yes — this is the primary deployment model (self-hosted NIM container on customer GPU hardware).
systems.tunables: start_history (default 300ms), start_th (default 0.2), stop_history (default 800ms), stop_th (default 0.98); VAD-based mode: enable_vad_endpointing flag, Silero onset (default 0.85) / offset (default 0.3).
systems.verification_note: Confirmed directly against docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/riva/user-guide/docs/asr/asr-pipeline-configuration.html, including default threshold values and the GPU-architecture-specific deployment warning.

systems.name: Ultravox (Fixie) — VAD Settings / turnEndpointDelay

systems.price_note: Not billed as a separate line item in the docs reviewed — vadSettings (turnEndpointDelay, minimumTurnDuration, minimumInterruptionDuration, frameActivationThreshold) are fields on Ultravox's Create Call API, included in standard call pricing.
systems.latency_note: turnEndpointDelay defaults to 0.384s (only multiples of 32ms are meaningful, per Ultravox's own docs); minimumInterruptionDuration defaults to 0.09s.
systems.accuracy_note: Not applicable — this is a VAD/turn-detection feature, not a transcription accuracy metric.
systems.languages_note: Not specified for VAD settings specifically in the pages reviewed; the separately open-sourced UltraVAD endpointing model is described elsewhere by Fixie as covering 26 languages, but that figure applies to the open model, not confirmed identical to the hosted API's default VAD.
systems.runs_on: Cloud API (real-time multimodal voice API)
systems.best_for: Developers who want granular, documented trade-off guidance on each individual VAD knob (turn delay, minimum turn duration, interruption sensitivity, frame-level activation threshold) rather than a single combined 'sensitivity' preset.
systems.watch: minimumInterruptionDuration is explicitly 'ignored if below minimumTurnDuration' — the two settings interact, so raising minimumTurnDuration without checking minimumInterruptionDuration can silently change interruption behavior in a way that isn't obvious from either setting alone.
systems.self_host: No for the hosted API; the underlying UltraVAD model has been released as open-weight separately by Fixie.
systems.tunables: turnEndpointDelay (default 0.384s, 32ms increments), minimumTurnDuration (default 0s), minimumInterruptionDuration (default 0.09s), frameActivationThreshold (0.1-1.0, default 0.1).
systems.verification_note: Confirmed directly against docs.ultravox.ai/noise/understanding-vad, including every default value listed.

systems.latency_note: end_of_turn_silence_ms defaults to 800ms, configurable from 500ms to 3,000ms.
systems.accuracy_note: Not applicable — this is an end-of-turn detection feature, not a transcription accuracy metric. Hume markets EVI's approach as using 'tone of voice' for end-of-turn detection, but publishes no separate precision/recall figure for the classifier in the pages reviewed.
systems.languages_note: Not specified for turn detection specifically in the pages reviewed.

systems.standout: Positions end-of-turn detection as 'the true bottleneck' EVI is built to solve, tying it explicitly to prosody/emotion signal rather than treating it as a bolt-on VAD component.

systems.verification_note: Confirmed directly against dev.hume.ai/docs/speech-to-speech-evi/configuration/turn-detection, including all three parameter defaults/ranges.

systems.accuracy_note: Not applicable — this is an endpointing feature, not a transcription accuracy metric.
systems.languages_note: Not specified for endpointing specifically in the pages reviewed.

systems.name: IBM Watson Speech to Text (end_of_phrase_silence_time)
systems.price_note: Not billed as a separate line item — end_of_phrase_silence_time and inactivity_timeout are recognize/streaming API parameters, included in standard Speech to Text plan pricing (Lite: 500 free minutes/month; Plus: usage-tiered per-minute rate; Premium: contact pricing), per IBM/third-party pricing summaries reviewed.
systems.latency_note: end_of_phrase_silence_time accepts 0.0-120.0 seconds; a value of 0 uses the service's language-specific default, documented as 0.8 seconds for most languages and 0.6 seconds for Chinese.
systems.accuracy_note: Not applicable — this is a phrase-segmentation/endpointing feature, not a transcription accuracy metric.
systems.languages_note: The default silence interval itself is language-dependent (0.8s for most languages, 0.6s for Chinese) — one of the only vendors in this set to document a locale-specific default rather than one global value.
systems.runs_on: Cloud API (Watson Speech to Text streaming/recognize)
systems.best_for: Applications needing fine control over how a long stream is split into multiple final transcript results based on pause length, distinct from the separate connection-level inactivity timeout.
systems.watch: end_of_phrase_silence_time (splits transcripts into results based on pauses) is easily confused with the separate inactivity_timeout parameter (closes the connection with a 400 error after silence, default 30s, or -1 for infinite) — they solve different problems and both need to be set correctly for a voice agent.
systems.standout: One of the few vendors reviewed whose documented endpointing default is explicitly language-conditional (0.8s vs. 0.6s for Chinese) rather than a single fixed value applied uniformly.
systems.billing_unit: per minute of audio (plan-tiered: Lite free tier, Plus per-minute, Premium contract)
systems.self_host: No — cloud API only (IBM also offers a separately-licensed on-prem Watson Speech to Text product not covered here).
systems.tunables: end_of_phrase_silence_time (0.0-120.0s; 0 = language-specific default), inactivity_timeout (seconds, default 30, or -1 for no timeout).
systems.verification_note: Parameter definition, ranges, and language-specific defaults confirmed against IBM's own Watson Developer Cloud Python SDK reference docs (an IBM-maintained official source); pricing tier figures are from third-party pricing summaries, not independently re-verified against IBM's own current pricing page in this pass.

Bland's own guidance is to start at 100 and adjust in ~10-point increments.

systems.name: Genesys Cloud (Barge-in / Speech Recognition Timeouts)
systems.price_note: Not billed as a separate line item — barge-in and speech-recognition timeout settings are Architect flow/bot configuration options within standard Genesys Cloud usage; no separate charge is documented for these settings specifically.
systems.latency_note: Not a single published number — three named, independently-configurable timeouts govern the interaction: how long to wait after the caller stops talking before accepting a valid match, how long to wait before declaring no-match on an invalid selection, and an overall deadline for the caller to respond before the system re-prompts or disconnects.
systems.accuracy_note: Not applicable — these are interaction-timing/barge-in features, not transcription accuracy metrics. Genesys separately exposes a minimum-confidence-level setting for matching, which is about NLU match confidence rather than turn-detection accuracy.
systems.languages_note: Not specified for these timeout settings specifically; Genesys's docs note settings 'trickle down to sub-menu levels unless overridden' across whatever languages the flow supports.
systems.runs_on: Cloud API (Genesys Cloud CX / Architect contact-center platform)
systems.best_for: Contact centers using Genesys Cloud's IVR/bot flows that need barge-in (letting callers interrupt a prompt) and separately-tunable no-input/no-match timeouts per menu or sub-menu.
systems.watch: This is scoped more narrowly than most rows here: what's documented is barge-in (interrupting prompt playback) and no-input/no-match response deadlines, not a dedicated ML end-of-turn classifier — treat this as classic IVR-style endpointing rather than a modern semantic turn-detection model.
systems.standout: Barge-in is on by default for essentially all prompt audio except Hold Music, and is configurable per individual queued prompt rather than only at the flow or menu level.
systems.billing_unit: Not disclosed for this feature specifically (bundled into standard Genesys Cloud CX licensing).
systems.self_host: No — cloud API/platform only.
systems.verification_note: Barge-in default behavior and the three named timeout settings read directly from help.genesys.cloud/articles/speech-recognition-overview/ (Genesys's own documentation); no independent measurement of timeout accuracy or false-trigger rate was performed.

gaps: No latency or accuracy figure anywhere in this matrix has been independently reproduced — every number, even on rows marked `verification: verified`, is the vendor's own self-reported benchmark or the vendor's own documented config default. "Verified" here means the parameter names and defaults were confirmed against a primary source, not that the number itself was checked by a third party.

Two turn-detector rows (Phoenix-VAD, Thai Semantic End-of-Turn Detection) are unreleased academic research with no public code, model, or dataset confirmed available — they are included because they are the only published work found on their respective angles (a dialogue-model-agnostic semantic endpointer; Thai-language end-of-turn detection), not because either is a usable system today.

Almost none of the commercial-api rows publish an accuracy or false-trigger rate for their own turn-detection feature — the pattern across that category is a documented config knob (a silence-duration default, a confidence threshold) with no measured detection-quality number attached. LiveKit Agents (orchestrator) is the only row in the whole matrix with a self-published, named-competitor benchmark for turn-detection quality itself.

Seven systems the original research brief named as "include at minimum" were researched but did not survive the audit, and are absent from this roster: Vocode, TEN Framework, Twilio, Vapi, ElevenLabs Conversational AI, SpeechBrain VAD, and NVIDIA NeMo/MarbleNet. OpenAI's own Realtime API is present only via the Azure-hosted variant (Azure OpenAI Realtime API), not as a direct OpenAI-hosted row. These are considered-and-not-found, not never-researched.

LiveKit's own turn-detector MODEL (Hugging Face livekit/turn-detector, ~0.1B parameters, a real, separately licensed, benchmarkable artifact distinct from the LiveKit Agents framework) is described only inside the LiveKit Agents (orchestrator) row's integration field and has no row of its own, so it is invisible to a reader filtering this matrix for turn-detector. It is independently notable enough to warrant one, but splitting it out requires new research beyond what this pass verified, so it stays folded into LiveKit Agents for now.
